issues.legal_issue: A married female who has a legal right of residence in a building falls within the inclusive definition of a landlord’s family and may be the beneficiary of an eviction claim based on her need.
material_facts: The landlord sought release of a tenanted shop so her daughter could expand a medical clinic being run from an adjacent shop.
The daughter was married and had inherited a share of the building from her deceased father, making her a co-owner.
The courts below found that the daughter needed the additional space for the clinic.
issues.conclusion: The married daughter was included in the definition of family because her inherited co-ownership gave her a legal right of residence in the building; the landlord could seek eviction for the daughter’s need.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(g) of the Uttar Pradesh Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 defines family inclusively and, in relation to a landlord, includes any female having a legal right of residence in the building, whether married or unmarried. Under Section 21(1)(a), the landlord may seek release for such a person’s bona fide need. The daughter inherited a share under the applicable Hanafi law of inheritance and, as a co-owner, had a legal right of residence.

predicates.rental_release_proceeding: A landlord sought release of a tenanted building or part of it for a claimed need.
predicates.female_need_beneficiary: The landlord claimed that a female needed the building or part of it.
predicates.beneficiary_has_legal_residence_right: The female beneficiary had a legal right to reside in the building.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks release for a female beneficiary who has a legal right to reside in the building, eviction for that beneficiary’s need is permitted.

issues.legal_issue: A supervisory court may not reverse concurrent factual findings in a rent-control eviction case merely by reappreciating the evidence when those findings are supported by the record and are not perverse or legally erroneous.
material_facts: The prescribed authority and the appellate court both found the landlord’s need for the adjacent shop to expand her daughter’s existing clinic to be bona fide.
Those courts found that the landlord had no other suitable shop, while the tenant had other shops in the same area to which he could move his business.
The High Court reconsidered the factual evidence and reversed the concurrent findings without finding them perverse, unsupported by evidence, or contrary to law.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction by reappreciating the evidence and reversing the concurrent findings; the eviction orders were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 does not confer appellate power to reassess evidence and reach different factual conclusions. Hindustan Petroleum Corpn. Ltd. v. Dilbahar Singh holds that factual findings may be corrected in rent-control supervisory or revisional jurisdiction when they are perverse, based on no evidence, reached without considering material evidence, based on misreading of evidence, or otherwise legally erroneous, but not merely because the reviewing court prefers a different view. The judgment also relies on Surya Dev Rai v. Ram Chander Rai concerning the limits of supervisory jurisdiction. In assessing need, the landlord is the sole judge of the space needed to start or expand an activity.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_writ_proceeding and concurrent_supported_findings and no_perversity_or_legal_error and high_court_reappraised_evidence

predicates.rent_control_eviction_writ_proceeding: A supervisory court reviewed a rent-control eviction decision in a writ proceeding.
predicates.concurrent_supported_findings: The lower decision-maker and the appellate court made the same factual findings, supported by the evidence they considered.
predicates.no_perversity_or_legal_error: The concurrent findings were not perverse, unsupported by evidence, or contrary to law.
predicates.high_court_reappraised_evidence: The supervisory court reweighed the evidence and reached different factual findings.

issues.definition: When a supervisory court reweighs evidence in a rent-control eviction proceeding despite supported concurrent findings that are not perverse or legally erroneous, reversing those findings is unjustified.
